title: Foraging young nettle tops in spring
subtitle: Safe harvest, handling, and cooking
excerpt: Stinging nettle young spring tops make a nutritious cooked green. Pick the top four to six leaves before the plant flowers. Cook before eating; the sting deactivates completely in heat or by thorough drying.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.

content.text: Stinging nettle (Urtica dioica) is a common UK hedgerow, field-margin, and waste-ground plant whose young spring tops make a cooked green with a flavour close to spinach. Pick the top four to six leaves per stem from March through May, before the plant flowers. Cook before eating; the sting deactivates completely in heat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification

: confirm (1) the toothed, heart-shaped leaf with a stinging surface, (2) the square stem covered in fine white hairs, and (3) the hedgerow, field margin, or disturbed ground habitat. All three must match.
ID features
Leaf: heart-shaped, deeply toothed, dark green, covered in fine stinging hairs. Stings on contact even through light fabric.
Stem: square in cross-section, covered in stinging hairs. Grows 0.5 to 1.5 m tall when established.
Habitat: hedgerow bases, field margins, waste ground, and riverbanks. Often grows in dense patches on nutrient-rich soil.
Season: young tops from March to May are best. After flowering (June onward) the leaves become tougher and develop gritty particles called cystoliths; stop harvesting when flowers appear.
Poisonous look-alikes
Stinging nettle has few dangerous
look-alike plants
in the UK, but two are worth knowing.
Dead nettle (Lamium species): similar toothed leaf but no sting and the stem is hollow. Dead nettles are edible but mild; avoid if you cannot confirm identification.
Hemp nettle (Galeopsis tetrahit): similar habitat, hairy stem, toothed leaf. No sting. Generally avoided rather than toxic; confirm the stinging surface before picking.
When and how to harvest

Pick from March to May, before the plant produces flowers. Wear gloves; kitchen rubber gloves or nitrile gloves work well. Use kitchen scissors to snip the top 10 to 15 cm of the stem, taking the youngest four to six leaves. Avoid plants on dog-walked paths, beside busy roads, or on land that may have been sprayed.
Take roughly a third of any patch and leave the rest to grow on.
After harvesting

Cook before eating; the sting deactivates completely in boiling water after about 30 seconds. Rinse in a colander with cold water while still wearing gloves, then drop straight into boiling salted water. The cooked green can be used in soup, as a steamed side, or in pasta. Use within 24 hours of picking.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of foliage from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Uprooting the plant is an offence.

rows.cause: Contact with the stinging hairs without gloves
rows.fix: Rinse with cool water. The sting subsides within 20 to 30 minutes. For future harvests, always wear gloves.

rows.cause: Not cooked long enough, or leaves were very mature
rows.fix: Blanch for at least 60 seconds in rapidly boiling water. Older leaves may need a full 2 minutes. Stop harvesting if the plant has flowered.

rows.cause: The plant has flowered and formed cystolith particles in the leaves
rows.fix: Stop harvesting once the plant shows flowers. Switch to a younger patch or wait until the following March.
